From Model Score to Campaign Decision vs. Third-Party Platform What’s Next (Part 2 Preview) Stories on how technology enables Swiggy to provide unparalleled convenience to consumers Decoding Customer Value: pLTV Models for India’s Quick Commerce Delivery Wars — part 1 Jayshmi A 9 min read · Jul 17, 2026 -- Listen Share Author: Jayshmi A Special thanks to soumyajyoti banerjee , Meghana Negi , Shaik Masihullah , Akash Deep for their contributions throughout this project and Sunil Rathee for his guidance. The counterintuitive story of how 350+ carefully engineered features + a simple MLP matched industry leaders and what that says about where the real moat lives in ML. Introduction Predicted lifetime value is one of the most fundamental signals in e-commerce. It quietly powers the long term growth by influencing: how platforms prioritize acquisition, how ad systems optimize bids, how retention programs decide whom to invest in, how incentives are allocated, and even how risk and fraud systems reason about customer quality over time. Underneath many of these decisions is the same question: not just will this user act , but how valuable are they likely to become? Most growth systems are optimized for the next action: a click, a cart, a first order. But for a marketplace like Swiggy — operating across two distinct verticals, food delivery and quick commerce (Instamart) , that is often too narrow. Two users can look nearly identical in the first few days after signup and still end up contributing very different long-term values. The install to purchase conversion rate in e-commerce is 1%-3%. This number is even smaller in the initial week or first few days. The system had to make high-stakes decisions in a setting where most users generated weak/no early signals, and where the business outcome we actually cared about ‘Lifetime Value’ appeared much later and was concentrated in a relatively small share of users. Our early attempts made this gap painfully visible. We started with an existing conversion-prediction model - the model produced predictions with a very high MAPE, meaning the predicted numbers were too noisy to put in a production system. This is a well-known challenge in the pLTV literature; point-estimate accuracy on heavily zero-inflated, long-tailed targets is notoriously difficult, and models trained for binary classification objectives (will this user convert?) don’t generalize to continuous value prediction (how much will this user be worth? - regression). The nuances of the Swiggy marketplace significantly amplify this challenge. The problem wasn’t producing a score; it was producing a score that could survive sparse early signals, distinguish high-value users from low-value ones early enough to change downstream decisions, and remain robust enough to plug into bidding systems. The Constraints: Why This Problem Is Hard The zero-inflation challenge. A large share of users place zero orders in their first 30 days. Any model that doesn’t explicitly handle this zero-mass will be systematically wrong, and a model that predicts “everyone is zero” will have a deceptively low MAE but zero business value. You can ace the loss function and still fail the business problem. Press enter or click to view image in full size Fig 1. Illustration of a typical LTV distribution as published in Google’s paper . Notice the large spike indicating zero or low ordering users. Multi-vertical complexity. A user’s value isn’t one number. They might be a weekly Instamart shopper who never orders Food, or a daily Food orderer who occasionally adds Instamart. The model needs to predict both independently. These two verticals have fundamentally different purchase patterns, zero-rates, and spend distributions but are also correlated by the same user behaviours. Cold-start at the worst possible moment. We predict soon after the user registers, much before the first order, with zero transaction history. The only signals possibly available are acquisition metadata, device characteristics, and geo-context. This is the hardest possible moment to make a lifetime value prediction, and also the moment when it matters most (ad platforms need the signal at install time to optimize bidding). The Swiggy market reality: two populations, one prediction target. Unlike mature e-commerce markets where most acquired users follow a broadly predictable spending trajectory, the Swiggy market is structurally different. A large share of new users are trial-motivated, they arrive through cashback offers, first-order discounts, or coupon-driven campaigns. They may look identical to genuine repeat buyers at day 1: same cart behavior, same session patterns, but their long-term trajectories might diverge. Press enter or click to view image in full size Fig 2. An Illustration of how LTV distribution might fit in an indian e-commerce setup. This means the model isn’t just predicting a continuous value from noisy features. It’s fundamentally trying to resolve two populations that are observationally similar at prediction time but behave completely differently over the 30-day horizon. If you get this wrong, you either bid aggressively for coupon-burners who will never return, or miss the genuine high-value users because their early signals looked unremarkable. Data richness as a double-edged sword. Swiggy’s data infrastructure is unusually rich, we don’t just have order history. We have address verification tags, phonetic name matching, geo-hierarchy competition metrics, post-order complaint dispositions by category, SKU-level Instamart category affinity, premium payment instrument usage, fraud signals, and acquisition channel attribution. All available before a single order is placed. The question wasn’t whether there was a signal; it was whether we could extract it without drowning in noise. The Feature Engineering Philosophy: Everything We Know, Encoded as Numbers We started with an audit. For every signal available before a user’s first order, we asked: does this correlate with LTV? If it did, it went in. The result was 350+ features across 12 groups. Our guiding principle was: everything we know, encoded as numbers. Here’s a look into some signals: 1. Acquisition Context Key Signals: Channel (organic, paid Food/IM, alliances, media partners). Strongest proxy for user intent — organic vs. paid-campaign installs tell fundamentally different stories about motivation. 2. Device & Fraud Key Signals: Jailbreak/GPS spoof/clone app/screen-sharing flags; sessions per device in 24h; payment carts per session.. Fraud signals double as LTV signals — a GPS spoofer is also a low-LTV user whose geo features are unreliable. 3. Geo-Hierarchy Key Signals: 4 spatial resolutions (Geohash-8 → Geohash-7 → Geohash-6 → city (building to neighbourhood to block to city): order share, discount rate, new-user density, competitor presence. 4. Post-Order Complaints Key Signals: Issue rates (missing items, quality, wrong items) at customer, device, and neighborhood level; 7/30/60-day lookbacks. 5. IM Category Affinity Key Signals: Order flags, counts, bills, cancellations, complaints per SKU category (F&V, Dairy, Cooking Essentials, Munchies, etc.) at customer + neighborhood level. Category mix is a retention signal — a weekly fresh-produce buyer has fundamentally different LTV than an occasional snack buyer, even at identical 7-day spend. 6. Last-X-Order Behavior Key Signals: Per-position features: vertical (IM vs Food), outcome, delivery fee paid, tip, inter-order intervals, complaint type, bill amount. Encodes behavioral trajectory without manual pattern definition i.e the shared trunk learns the sequences. 7. Affluence & Socioeconomic Key Signals: Premium/gourmet restaurant orders; delivery fee paid without subscription; address tags (apartments, tech parks); premium payment instruments; corporate meal cards. 8. Phonetic Name & Address Matching Key Signals: Same-sounding names in neighborhood: order volume, cancellation rate, complaint rate; similar-sounding address landmarks. Catches household-level signals that individual-level features miss — shared buildings where address strings vary (“Flat 3B, XYZ Apts” vs “XYZ Apartments, 3rd Floor”). 9. Cart Drop-Off & Misc Key Signals: COD abandonment ratio; lifetime order aggregates; temporal features (hour of day, day of week). COD drop-off signals payment friction that directly affects completion rates and therefore LTV. In total: 10+ feature groups, 350+ features, every signal we could extract before the first order. Press enter or click to view image in full size Fig 3. Feature importance across multiple categories used in LTV prediction. Spotlights Geo-Hierarchy : Four Resolutions, Four Different Questions — A user’s location is represented at four spatial scales simultaneously. Geohash-8: new-user intensity at the apartment. Geohash-7: Instamart order share, discount rate, new-user density, 7-day transacting users. Geohash-6: total and completed orders at 7- and 30-day windows, competitor order share. City: new-user order volume, 7-day window. The ratio of block-level to neighborhood-level orders tells the model how “concentrated” demand is around this specific user. A micro-cluster signal that city-level trends completely miss. A user in a building with high Instamart penetration surrounded by a neighborhood with low penetration is a different signal than either dimension alone. Post-Order Complaints : Three Levels, One Powerful Signal — Complaint data (missing items, quality issues, wrong items) aggregated at three levels: Customer: What share of this user’s past orders had issues? Device: What’s the issue rate on this specific device? Catches shared-device patterns if this phone has complaints across multiple Swiggy accounts, that’s a signal about the user behind it. Neighborhood: What’s the local issue rate, broken down by Food vs. IM? A user with a complaint history will likely churn regardless of individual spend as bad experiences drive abandonment. A neighborhood with high refund-to-bill ratios signals systematic delivery quality issues that depress LTV for everyone there. The Model Architecture: Given the richness of the features, we deliberately kept the model architecture simple. Press enter or click to view image in full size Fig 4. Model Architecture Three shared hidden layers, two task-specific heads. No attention, no embeddings, no mixture-of-experts, no transformers. Trained with a custom MAE loss, Adam optimizer. The 4-Head Insight: Auxiliary Tasks as Free Regularization As we iterated, we experimented with expanding to four heads, adding order-count predictions alongside LTV for each vertical. The intuition was that predicting how many orders a user would place (a frequency signal) might help the shared trunk learn richer representations than predicting how much LTV (a magnitude signal) alone. We also experimented narrowing the trunk as order-count heads would provide intermediate supervision. The results surprised us: the 4-head model achieved marginally better performance while using 63% fewer parameters (135K vs 363K) Press enter or click to view image in full size Table 1. Comparision of 2-head (LTV only) vs 4-head (LTV + order frequency) models. (Part 2 of this series will cover the evolution to probabilistic model architectures) Results Why Not Just Report MAE? A natural first instinct is to by MAE, MAPE, R². The problem is that these metrics are deeply misleading on zero-inflated LTV targets. >50% of new users place no orders in a typical e-commerce market. A model that simply predicts zero for everyone achieves a better MAE than most non-trivial models while being completely useless for campaign targeting. High MAPE on non-zero actuals is almost guaranteed even for a good model, because LTV distributions have heavy tails where a single outlier user can swing a percentage error by orders of magnitude. Practically Meaningful Eval Can the model correctly rank users by their relative value? Ad platforms don’t need the exact value but to say “this user is in the top 20% so bid higher for them.” So we evaluate via quantile matching and diagonal coverage along with a spearman coefficient : sort users by predicted and true labels into 10 equal buckets; check how much of the population lands in the right bucket. A random model scores 10% diagonal. The goal is to push that as high as possible, especially at the extremes. We are able to achieve >0.75 spearman in IM and Food respectively, with diagonal coverage of 70–80%. Press enter or click to view image in full size Fig 5. Illustration of a heatmap used to measure diagonal coverage of population for whom predicted LTV sits in the right decile. From Model Score to Campaign Decision The model’s role in production is to feed directly into Google’s tROAS bidding. The causal chain is: better rank ordering → correct bid differentiation → more budget allocated to acquirable high-value users → better cohort quality at the same spend. vs. Third-Party Platform The real test came when we ran A/B experiments pitting against an external pLTV bidding platform. The results: Press enter or click to view image in full size Table 2. Comparision of in-house pLTV model against a third-party vendor when used in a production system for ads bidding. Our in-house model delivered better retention and higher gross order value per acquired user at zero incremental platform cost. The third-party platform acquired more new users per dollar spent (their campaign was more volume-efficient). What’s Next (Part 2 Preview) In Part 2, we’ll cover the model’s evolution from MAE-based point predictions to a probabilistic architecture. This moves the model from “what’s the expected value?” to “what’s the full probability distribution?” enabling the ad platform to make risk-aware bidding decisions in real time. We’ll also dive deeper into the trade-offs, the Kendall uncertainty weighting scheme for multi-task balancing and model metrics. -- -- Written by Jayshmi A 7 followers · 1 following Published in Swiggy Bytes — Tech Blog 12.5K followers · Last published Jul 17, 2026 Stories on how technology enables Swiggy to provide unparalleled convenience to consumers Help Status About Careers Press Blog Store Privacy Rules Terms Text to speech
